claim: A light-sensitive variant of EB1 was developed by inserting a blue light-controlled protein dimerization module between functional domains.
source: We previously developed a light-sensitive variant of the microtubule plus end-tracking protein EB1 by inserting a blue light-controlled protein dimerization module between functional domains.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a previously developed method.

claim: Endogenous EB1 can be replaced with a light-sensitive variant in a single genome editing step.
source: Here, we describe an advanced method to replace endogenous EB1 with this light-sensitive variant in a single genome editing step, thereby enabling this approach in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) and hiPSC-derived neurons.
evidence: This is the primary methodological claim of the manuscript, stated in the abstract.

claim: Acute and local optogenetic EB1 inactivation in developing cortical neurons induces microtubule depolymerization in the growth cone periphery.
source: We demonstrate that acute and local optogenetic EB1 inactivation in developing cortical neurons induces microtubule depolymerization in the growth cone periphery and subsequent neurite retraction.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Acute and local optogenetic EB1 inactivation in developing cortical neurons induces subsequent neurite retraction.
source: We demonstrate that acute and local optogenetic EB1 inactivation in developing cortical neurons induces microtubule depolymerization in the growth cone periphery and subsequent neurite retraction.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Advancing growth cones are repelled from areas of blue light exposure in π-EB1 neurons.
source: In addition, advancing growth cones are repelled from areas of blue light exposure.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The phenotypes of EB1 photoinactivation were independent of the neuronal EB1 homolog EB3.
source: These phenotypes were independent of the neuronal EB1 homolog EB3, revealing a direct dynamic role of EB1-mediated microtubule plus end interactions in neuron morphogenesis and neurite guidance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments using EB3 knockout cells shown in Figures 2-5.

claim: EB1-mediated microtubule plus end interactions play a direct dynamic role in neuron morphogenesis.
source: These phenotypes were independent of the neuronal EB1 homolog EB3, revealing a direct dynamic role of EB1-mediated microtubule plus end interactions in neuron morphogenesis and neurite guidance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing effects of EB1 photoinactivation.

claim: EB1-mediated microtubule plus end interactions play a direct dynamic role in neurite guidance.
source: These phenotypes were independent of the neuronal EB1 homolog EB3, revealing a direct dynamic role of EB1-mediated microtubule plus end interactions in neuron morphogenesis and neurite guidance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing growth cone repulsion from blue light.

claim: Microtubules are essential components of the cytoskeleton in mature neurons where polarized MT tracks support axonal transport.
source: Microtubules (MTs) are essential components of the cytoskeleton in both mature neurons, in which polarized MT tracks support axonal transport, as well as during nervous system development (Atkins et al., 2023; Kapitein and Hoogenraad, 2015; van de Willige et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Microtubules are essential components of the cytoskeleton during nervous system development.
source: Microtubules (MTs) are essential components of the cytoskeleton in both mature neurons, in which polarized MT tracks support axonal transport, as well as during nervous system development (Atkins et al., 2023; Kapitein and Hoogenraad, 2015; van de Willige et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: During neuronal differentiation, the expression of many microtubule-associated proteins is upregulated.
source: During neuronal differentiation, the expression of many microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) is upregulated, and numerous neurodevelopmental diseases are being linked to genetic alterations in MAPs, MT motors, and tubulin itself (Franker and Hoogenraad, 2013; Maillard et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Numerous neurodevelopmental diseases are being linked to genetic alterations in MAPs, MT motors, and tubulin.
source: During neuronal differentiation, the expression of many microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) is upregulated, and numerous neurodevelopmental diseases are being linked to genetic alterations in MAPs, MT motors, and tubulin itself (Franker and Hoogenraad, 2013; Maillard et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neurite growth and pathfinding are driven by adhesion and F-actin dynamics in the growth cone.
source: Neurite growth and pathfinding are driven by adhesion and F-actin dynamics in the growth cone, the advancing terminal structure of growing neurites.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Dynamic MTs enter the F-actin rich growth cone periphery and these 'pioneer' MTs participate in growth cone advance and guidance downstream of extracellular cues.
source: Analogous to the role of MTs in migrating cells, dynamic MTs enter the F-actin rich growth cone periphery and these so-called 'pioneer' MTs participate in growth cone advance and guidance downstream of extracellular cues (Liu and Dwyer, 2014; Vitriol and Zheng, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Proteins that associate with growing MT plus ends (+TIPs) play critical roles in neuron morphogenesis.
source: Proteins that associate with growing MT plus ends (+TIPs), such as spectraplakins (MACF1), the adenomatous polyposis coli protein APC, CLASPs, and neuron navigator proteins (Nav1), play critical roles in neuron morphogenesis (Cammarata et al., 2016; Coles and Bradke, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Nav1 mediates interactions between dynamic MT plus ends and F-actin filaments.
source: For example, Nav1 mediates interactions between dynamic MT plus ends and F-actin filaments (Sánchez-Huertas et al., 2020) and CLASPs are involved in cell-matrix adhesion site remodeling (Stehbens et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: CLASPs are involved in cell-matrix adhesion site remodeling.
source: For example, Nav1 mediates interactions between dynamic MT plus ends and F-actin filaments (Sánchez-Huertas et al., 2020) and CLASPs are involved in cell-matrix adhesion site remodeling (Stehbens et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: +TIPs bind to growing MT plus ends through small adaptor proteins of the end-binding (EB) family.
source: These +TIPs bind to growing MT plus ends through small adaptor proteins of the end-binding (EB) family.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: In humans, EBs are encoded by three MAPRE genes.
source: In humans, EBs are encoded by three MAPRE genes, and although EB1 is the best characterized +TIP adaptor, it remains unclear to what extent EB functions overlap.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: EB1 is the best characterized +TIP adaptor.
source: In humans, EBs are encoded by three MAPRE genes, and although EB1 is the best characterized +TIP adaptor, it remains unclear to what extent EB functions overlap.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: It remains unclear to what extent EB functions overlap.
source: In humans, EBs are encoded by three MAPRE genes, and although EB1 is the best characterized +TIP adaptor, it remains unclear to what extent EB functions overlap.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: EB3 is upregulated in neurons and other differentiated cell types.
source: For example, EB3, which is upregulated in neurons and other differentiated cell types, coordinates MT and F-actin dynamics in developing neurons independent of EB1 (Gordon-Weeks, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: EB3 coordinates MT and F-actin dynamics in developing neurons independent of EB1.
source: For example, EB3, which is upregulated in neurons and other differentiated cell types, coordinates MT and F-actin dynamics in developing neurons independent of EB1 (Gordon-Weeks, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The role of EB1-dependent +TIPs in neuron morphogenesis is inferred mostly from genetic knockout phenotypes in model systems from different species.
source: The role of EB1-dependent+TIPs in neuron morphogenesis is inferred mostly from genetic knockout phenotypes in model systems from different species.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous research in the introduction.

claim: It has not been tested how +TIP association with growing MT ends participates in controlling growth cone dynamics in real time in developing human neurons.
source: It has not been tested how +TIP association with growing MT ends participates in controlling growth cone dynamics in real time in developing human neurons in part due to an absence of technology to acutely inhibit these interactions.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: The absence of technology to acutely inhibit +TIP interactions has prevented testing how +TIP association with growing MT ends participates in controlling growth cone dynamics in real time.
source: It has not been tested how +TIP association with growing MT ends participates in controlling growth cone dynamics in real time in developing human neurons in part due to an absence of technology to acutely inhibit these interactions.
evidence: This is stated as a technological limitation that the current study addresses.

claim: EB1 is necessary to stabilize MTs in the growth cone periphery.
source: In addition to demonstrating a novel strategy to generate photosensitive variants of multidomain proteins in a single genome editing step, we show that EB1 is necessary to stabilize MTs in the growth cone periphery and to maintain growth cone advance, and that this function of EB1 cannot be compensated by EB3.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: EB1 is necessary to maintain growth cone advance.
source: In addition to demonstrating a novel strategy to generate photosensitive variants of multidomain proteins in a single genome editing step, we show that EB1 is necessary to stabilize MTs in the growth cone periphery and to maintain growth cone advance, and that this function of EB1 cannot be compensated by EB3.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: The function of EB1 in stabilizing MTs in the growth cone periphery and maintaining growth cone advance cannot be compensated by EB3.
source: In addition to demonstrating a novel strategy to generate photosensitive variants of multidomain proteins in a single genome editing step, we show that EB1 is necessary to stabilize MTs in the growth cone periphery and to maintain growth cone advance, and that this function of EB1 cannot be compensated by EB3.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the introduction and supported by experiments using EB3 knockout cells.

claim: AlphaFold2 does not correctly predict relative domain positions in the π-EB1 tetramer.
source: Note that AlphaFold2 does not correctly predict relative domain positions and did not capture the LOV2/Zdk1 interaction correctly although a structure of the LOV2/Zdk1 dimer has previously been determined (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the AlphaFold2 model shown in Figure 1A.

claim: AlphaFold2 did not capture the LOV2/Zdk1 interaction correctly.
source: Note that AlphaFold2 does not correctly predict relative domain positions and did not capture the LOV2/Zdk1 interaction correctly although a structure of the LOV2/Zdk1 dimer has previously been determined (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the AlphaFold2 model shown in Figure 1A, with reference to a previous structure determination.

claim: A structure of the LOV2/Zdk1 dimer has previously been determined.
source: Note that AlphaFold2 does not correctly predict relative domain positions and did not capture the LOV2/Zdk1 interaction correctly although a structure of the LOV2/Zdk1 dimer has previously been determined (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Homozygous integration of a π-element with an internal EF1α promoter driving expression of the C-terminal π-EB1 half resulted in balanced expression of both π-EB1 parts.
source: Evaluating different designs of what we named π-elements in H1299 human cancer cells, we found that homozygous integration of a π-element in which an internal EF1α promoter drives expression of the C-terminal π-EB1 half while the N-terminal half remains under the control of the endogenous promoter (Figure 1B) resulted in balanced expression of both π-EB1 parts and in homozygous edited clones yielded π-EB1 protein levels that were similar to EB1 in control cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Homozygous edited clones with the EF1α π-element yielded π-EB1 protein levels that were similar to EB1 in control cells.
source: Evaluating different designs of what we named π-elements in H1299 human cancer cells, we found that homozygous integration of a π-element in which an internal EF1α promoter drives expression of the C-terminal π-EB1 half while the N-terminal half remains under the control of the endogenous promoter (Figure 1B) resulted in balanced expression of both π-EB1 parts and in homozygous edited clones yielded π-EB1 protein levels that were similar to EB1 in control cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: An internal ribosome entry site (IRES) resulted in very poor expression of the C-terminal half of π-EB1.
source: In contrast, an internal ribosome entry site (IRES) resulted in very poor expression of the C-terminal half.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Self-cleaving 2A peptides did not work for π-element design because the C-terminus of the LOV2 domain cannot be modified without greatly inhibiting Zdk1 binding.
source: Of note, self-cleaving 2 A peptides also did not work because the C-terminus of the LOV2 domain cannot be modified without greatly inhibiting Zdk1 binding (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a design constraint with reference to previous literature.

claim: i3N cells are an hiPSC line that expresses Ngn2 under the control of a doxycycline-induced promoter to allow inducible differentiation into cortical glutamatergic i3Neurons.
source: We next tested π-element integration in i3N cells, an hiPSC line that expresses Ngn2 under the control of a doxycycline-induced promoter to allow inducible differentiation into cortical glutamatergic i3Neurons (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the cell line used, supported by a citation.

claim: Homozygous π-element integration into both copies of exon 5 of the endogenous MAPRE1 (EB1) gene was validated by genomic PCR, sequencing, and immunoblot.
source: Homozygous π-element integration into both copies of exon 5 of the endogenous MAPRE1 (EB1) gene was validated by genomic PCR, sequencing, and immunoblot (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: EB1N-LOV2 expression levels were similar to EB1 in control cells and only mildly reduced in both i3N hiPSCs and i3Neurons.
source: Because the N-terminal π-EB1 half is expressed from the endogenous EB1 promoter, compared with EB1 in control cells, EB1N-LOV2 expression levels were similar and only mildly reduced in both i3N hiPSCs and i3Neurons (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Expression of Zdk1-EB1C driven by the EF1α promoter was markedly increased in i3N hiPSCs but was lower in i3Neurons.
source: In contrast, expression of Zdk1-EB1C that is driven by the EF1α promoter was markedly increased in i3N hiPSCs but was lower in i3Neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The change in Zdk1-EB1C expression indicates a change in the activity balance of the endogenous EB1 and EF1α promoters during i3N neuronal differentiation.
source: This indicates a change in the activity balance of these two promoters during i3N neuronal differentiation and suggests that the π-element design could be improved by also using the native promotor to drive expression of the C-terminal half.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the expression data in Figure 1D.

claim: The π-element design could be improved by also using the native promotor to drive expression of the C-terminal half.
source: This indicates a change in the activity balance of these two promoters during i3N neuronal differentiation and suggests that the π-element design could be improved by also using the native promotor to drive expression of the C-terminal half.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future improvement based on the observed expression patterns.

source: However, we did not try this, because proliferation, stem cell properties (Figure 1F), and most importantly differentiation into i3Neurons appeared normal as indicated by expected changes in expression levels of marker proteins such as EB3, DCX, and KIF2C that increase or decrease, respectively, during neuronal differentiation (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B) (Blair et al., 2017).

claim: Stem cell properties of π-EB1 i3N hiPSCs appeared normal.
source: However, we did not try this, because proliferation, stem cell properties (Figure 1F), and most importantly differentiation into i3Neurons appeared normal as indicated by expected changes in expression levels of marker proteins such as EB3, DCX, and KIF2C that increase or decrease, respectively, during neuronal differentiation (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B) (Blair et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by Oct4 staining shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Differentiation of π-EB1 i3N hiPSCs into i3Neurons appeared normal as indicated by expected changes in expression levels of marker proteins such as EB3, DCX, and KIF2C.
source: However, we did not try this, because proliferation, stem cell properties (Figure 1F), and most importantly differentiation into i3Neurons appeared normal as indicated by expected changes in expression levels of marker proteins such as EB3, DCX, and KIF2C that increase or decrease, respectively, during neuronal differentiation (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B) (Blair et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1D and ribosome profiling data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B, with reference to previous literature.

claim: EB1 and EB3 are very similar and may be at least partially functionally redundant.
source: Because EB1 and EB3 are very similar and may be at least partially functionally redundant, we also removed EB3 expression by introducing a frameshift and premature stop codon near the start of the EB3 open reading frame in π-EB1 i3N hiPSCs (Figure 1H; Figure 1—figure supplement 3) to be able to ask how EB1 contributes to neuron morphogenesis and compare the relative contributions of EB1 and EB3.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for generating EB3 knockout cells.

claim: EB3 expression was removed by introducing a frameshift and premature stop codon near the start of the EB3 open reading frame in π-EB1 i3N hiPSCs.
source: Because EB1 and EB3 are very similar and may be at least partially functionally redundant, we also removed EB3 expression by introducing a frameshift and premature stop codon near the start of the EB3 open reading frame in π-EB1 i3N hiPSCs (Figure 1H; Figure 1—figure supplement 3) to be able to ask how EB1 contributes to neuron morphogenesis and compare the relative contributions of EB1 and EB3.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Clonal π-EB1 i3N hiPSC colonies homogenously expressed EGFP-Zdk1-EB1C.
source: Clonal π-EB1 i3N hiPSC colonies homogenously expressed EGFP-Zdk1-EB1C, and as expected, EGFP-Zdk1-EB1C rapidly dissociated from growing MT ends during blue light exposure in both i3N stem cells (Figure 1G) and differentiating i3Neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: EGFP-Zdk1-EB1C rapidly dissociated from growing MT ends during blue light exposure in i3N stem cells.
source: Clonal π-EB1 i3N hiPSC colonies homogenously expressed EGFP-Zdk1-EB1C, and as expected, EGFP-Zdk1-EB1C rapidly dissociated from growing MT ends during blue light exposure in both i3N stem cells (Figure 1G) and differentiating i3Neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: EGFP-Zdk1-EB1C rapidly dissociated from growing MT ends during blue light exposure in differentiating i3Neurons.
source: Clonal π-EB1 i3N hiPSC colonies homogenously expressed EGFP-Zdk1-EB1C, and as expected, EGFP-Zdk1-EB1C rapidly dissociated from growing MT ends during blue light exposure in both i3N stem cells (Figure 1G) and differentiating i3Neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: π-EB1 photoinactivation significantly attenuated MT growth in i3N hiPSCs.
source: In addition, and similar to what we previously observed in interphase human cancer cells (van Haren et al., 2018), π-EB1 photoinactivation significantly attenuated MT growth in i3N hiPSCs transiently expressing EB1N-mScarlet-LOV2, which remains on MT ends and enables MT growth rate measurements before and during blue light exposure (Figure 1I and J, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I and J, and is consistent with previous observations.

claim: π-EB1 EB3-/- i3Neurons sprouted neurites normally upon Ngn2-induced differentiation.
source: Upon Ngn2-induced differentiation, π-EB1 EB3-/- i3Neurons sprouted neurites normally (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D, Figure 1—video 2), and as expected, the EGFP-tagged C-terminal half of π-EB1 associated with growing MT ends in neurites with the majority of growing MT ends localized to growth cones.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The EGFP-tagged C-terminal half of π-EB1 associated with growing MT ends in neurites with the majority of growing MT ends localized to growth cones.
source: Upon Ngn2-induced differentiation, π-EB1 EB3-/- i3Neurons sprouted neurites normally (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D, Figure 1—video 2), and as expected, the EGFP-tagged C-terminal half of π-EB1 associated with growing MT ends in neurites with the majority of growing MT ends localized to growth cones.
evidence: This is an observation from imaging experiments.

claim: MT growth is slower in neurons than in proliferating cells.
source: Of note, because MT growth is slower in neurons than in proliferating cells (Stepanova et al., 2003), EGFP-Zdk1-EB1C comets were less elongated in i3Neurons and appeared more punctate compared with i3N hiPSCs.
evidence: This is stated with reference to previous literature.

claim: EGFP-Zdk1-EB1C comets were less elongated in i3Neurons and appeared more punctate compared with i3N hiPSCs.
source: Of note, because MT growth is slower in neurons than in proliferating cells (Stepanova et al., 2003), EGFP-Zdk1-EB1C comets were less elongated in i3Neurons and appeared more punctate compared with i3N hiPSCs.
evidence: This is an observation explained by the slower MT growth in neurons.

claim: EGFP-Zdk1-EB1C quickly and reversibly dissociated from MT ends upon blue light exposure in π-EB1 EB3-/- i3Neurons.
source: Nevertheless, EGFP-Zdk1-EB1C quickly and reversibly dissociated from MT ends upon blue light exposure in π-EB1 EB3-/- i3Neurons (Figure 2A, Figure 2—video 1).

claim: In control i3Neuron growth cones, MTs dynamically extended from the central domain into the growth cone periphery.
source: In control i3Neuron growth cones, MTs dynamically extended from the central domain into the growth cone periphery and the average length of these MTs was not affected by blue light.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The average length of MTs in control i3Neuron growth cones was not affected by blue light.
source: In control i3Neuron growth cones, MTs dynamically extended from the central domain into the growth cone periphery and the average length of these MTs was not affected by blue light.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: In π-EB1 i3Neurons, MTs in the growth cone periphery frequently shortened in response to blue light exposure.
source: In contrast, in π-EB1 i3Neurons MTs in the growth cone periphery frequently shortened in response to blue light exposure (Figure 2B and C; Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: π-EB1 photoinactivation-induced MT shortening was most pronounced in π-EB1 EB3-/- i3Neurons.
source: While π-EB1 photoinactivation-induced MT shortening was most pronounced in π-EB1 EB3-/- i3Neurons, MTs also shortened in π-EB1 i3Neurons that still expressed EB3 and in both cases the relative MT length after 20 s of blue light was significantly reduced compared with control i3Neurons (p<0.001 by ANOVA and Tukey-Kramer HSD).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MTs shortened in π-EB1 i3Neurons that still expressed EB3 in response to blue light exposure.
source: While π-EB1 photoinactivation-induced MT shortening was most pronounced in π-EB1 EB3-/- i3Neurons, MTs also shortened in π-EB1 i3Neurons that still expressed EB3 and in both cases the relative MT length after 20 s of blue light was significantly reduced compared with control i3Neurons (p<0.001 by ANOVA and Tukey-Kramer HSD).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The relative MT length after 20 s of blue light was significantly reduced in both π-EB1 and π-EB1 EB3-/- i3Neurons compared with control i3Neurons.
source: While π-EB1 photoinactivation-induced MT shortening was most pronounced in π-EB1 EB3-/- i3Neurons, MTs also shortened in π-EB1 i3Neurons that still expressed EB3 and in both cases the relative MT length after 20 s of blue light was significantly reduced compared with control i3Neurons (p<0.001 by ANOVA and Tukey-Kramer HSD).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Taxane-based probes label growing MT ends more dimly than the rest of the MT possibly due to slow redistribution kinetics on MTs in cells.
source: Although taxane-based probes label growing MT ends more dimly than the rest of the MT possibly due to slow redistribution kinetics on MTs in cells (Ettinger et al., 2016), we were able to measure growth cone MT polymerization rates during blue light exposure by manual tracking MT length changes.
evidence: This is stated as an observation with reference to previous literature.

claim: Absolute MT growth rates measured using taxane-based probes are underestimated due to reduced temporal resolution compared with EB1 tracking.
source: Even though MT growth rates in neurons are lower compared with other cells (Stepanova et al., 2003), it is important to note that absolute MT growth rates in this experiment are further underestimated because of the reduced temporal resolution compared with EB1 tracking (Gierke et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological limitation with references to previous literature.

claim: After 1 min of blue light exposure, growth cone MT growth rates in both π-EB1 lines were reduced at least fourfold compared with control i3Neurons.
source: Nevertheless, compared with control i3Neurons, after 1 min of blue light exposure, growth cone MT growth rates in both π-EB1 lines were reduced at least fourfold (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: EB1-mediated MT end interactions are required to stabilize and sustain net growth cone MT growth.
source: Thus, taken together these data show that EB1-mediated MT end interactions are required to stabilize and sustain net growth cone MT growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Endogenous EB3 cannot compensate for the acute loss of EB1 function in i3Neuron growth cones.
source: In addition, our results indicate that endogenous EB3 cannot compensate for the acute loss of EB1 function in i3Neuron growth cones.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing π-EB1 and π-EB1 EB3-/- i3Neurons.

claim: π-EB1 photoinactivation can partially displace EB3 from growing MT ends.
source: Because we previously observed that π-EB1 photoinactivation can partially displace EB3 from growing MT ends (van Haren et al., 2018), we cannot completely exclude a dominant negative effect of π-EB1 photoinactivation on EB3.
evidence: This is stated with reference to previous observations.

claim: A dominant negative effect of π-EB1 photoinactivation on EB3 cannot be completely excluded.
source: Because we previously observed that π-EB1 photoinactivation can partially displace EB3 from growing MT ends (van Haren et al., 2018), we cannot completely exclude a dominant negative effect of π-EB1 photoinactivation on EB3.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat to the interpretation of the results.

claim: EB1N-LOV2 likely does not interfere with EB3 binding to MTs by direct competition for binding sites because the EB1N-LOV2 expression level in i3Neurons is below that of EB1 in control cells.
source: However, because the EB1N-LOV2 expression level in i3Neurons is below that of EB1 in control cells, EB1N-LOV2 likely does not interfere with EB3 binding to MTs by direct competition for binding sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression level data.

claim: The findings are consistent with not fully understood functional differences between EB1 and EB3 in developing neurons that relate both to their binding sites on MT ends as well as differences in interaction partners.
source: Our findings are however consistent with not fully understood functional differences between EB1 and EB3 in developing neurons that relate both to their binding sites on MT ends as well as differences in interaction partners.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the results in the context of existing knowledge.

claim: EB3 trails behind EB1 on growing MT ends.
source: Specifically, EB3 trails behind EB1 on growing MT ends and only EB3 binds to the F-actin regulator drebrin possibly coordinating F-actin and MT dynamics independently of directly controlling MT growth (Poobalasingam et al., 2022; Roth et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with reference to previous literature.

claim: Only EB3 binds to the F-actin regulator drebrin.
source: Specifically, EB3 trails behind EB1 on growing MT ends and only EB3 binds to the F-actin regulator drebrin possibly coordinating F-actin and MT dynamics independently of directly controlling MT growth (Poobalasingam et al., 2022; Roth et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with reference to previous literature.

claim: EB3 binding to drebrin possibly coordinates F-actin and MT dynamics independently of directly controlling MT growth.
source: Specifically, EB3 trails behind EB1 on growing MT ends and only EB3 binds to the F-actin regulator drebrin possibly coordinating F-actin and MT dynamics independently of directly controlling MT growth (Poobalasingam et al., 2022; Roth et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a possibility with reference to previous literature.

claim: EB3 may be more important during later stages of neuron development when EB3 is more highly expressed.

evidence: This is stated as an alternative explanation with reference to previous literature.

claim: 'Pioneer' MTs that enter the growth cone periphery participate in growth cone guidance.
source: Because 'pioneer' MTs that enter the growth cone periphery participate in growth cone guidance (Buck and Zheng, 2002), and MT and F-actin dynamics are coupled both mechanically and biochemically through Rho GTPase signaling, we next asked how π-EB1 photoinactivation affected F-actin dynamics.
evidence: This is stated with reference to previous literature.

claim: MT and F-actin dynamics are coupled both mechanically and biochemically through Rho GTPase signaling.
source: Because 'pioneer' MTs that enter the growth cone periphery participate in growth cone guidance (Buck and Zheng, 2002), and MT and F-actin dynamics are coupled both mechanically and biochemically through Rho GTPase signaling, we next asked how π-EB1 photoinactivation affected F-actin dynamics.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: MT growth is thought to activate Rac1 which drives leading-edge actin polymerization.
source: MT growth is thought to activate Rac1 which drives leading-edge actin polymerization, while MT shortening activates RhoA that increases actomyosin contractility through the release of regulatory MT-bound factors (Garcin and Straube, 2019; Wittmann and Waterman-Storer, 2001).
evidence: This is stated with reference to previous literature.

claim: MT shortening activates RhoA that increases actomyosin contractility through the release of regulatory MT-bound factors.

claim: The F-actin retrograde flow rate in control i3Neurons was 2.8+/-0.4 µm/min.
source: On kymographs perpendicular to the growth cone edge (Figure 3B), we measured the same F-actin retrograde flow rate in control (2.8+/-0.4 µm/min; mean +/-standard deviation) and π-EB1 EB3-/- i3Neurons (2.8+/-0.3 µm/min) in the dark, similar to previous measurements in growth cones from other vertebrate species (Flynn et al., 2012; Geraldo and Gordon-Weeks, 2009; Gomez and Letourneau, 2014).
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The growth cone F-actin retrograde flow rate remained remarkably constant during blue light exposure.
source: Although growth cone morphology was highly dynamic (Figure 3—video 1), the growth cone F-actin retrograde flow rate remained remarkably constant during blue light exposure (Figure 3C), and we also did not observe consistent changes in overall F-actin dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No consistent changes in overall F-actin dynamics were observed during blue light exposure.
source: Although growth cone morphology was highly dynamic (Figure 3—video 1), the growth cone F-actin retrograde flow rate remained remarkably constant during blue light exposure (Figure 3C), and we also did not observe consistent changes in overall F-actin dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: Retrograde F-actin flow is directly related to the rate of leading-edge actin polymerization.
source: Because retrograde F-actin flow is directly related to the rate of leading-edge actin polymerization, this indicates that EB1-mediated MT growth or +TIP interactions do not immediately influence growth cone actin polymerization dynamics.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: EB1-mediated MT growth or +TIP interactions do not immediately influence growth cone actin polymerization dynamics.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the F-actin flow data in Figure 3.

claim: Within a 15 min observation window, >90% of π-EB1 neurites visibly retracted when the entire growth cone was exposed to blue light.
source: Within a 15 min observation window, >90% of π-EB1 neurites visibly retracted when the entire growth cone was exposed to blue light (Figure 4A and B; Figure 4—video 1), regardless of whether these cells expressed EB3 or not, again indicating that EB3 is not able to compensate for the acute loss of EB1 function in early neurite development.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The retraction of π-EB1 neurites occurred regardless of whether these cells expressed EB3 or not.
source: Within a 15 min observation window, >90% of π-EB1 neurites visibly retracted when the entire growth cone was exposed to blue light (Figure 4A and B; Figure 4—video 1), regardless of whether these cells expressed EB3 or not, again indicating that EB3 is not able to compensate for the acute loss of EB1 function in early neurite development.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing π-EB1 and π-EB1 EB3-/- i3Neurons.

claim: EB3 is not able to compensate for the acute loss of EB1 function in early neurite development.

claim: Only ~40% of control i3Neuron neurites shortened during blue light exposure.
source: In contrast and as expected, control i3Neurons were insensitive to blue light exposure with only ~40% of neurites shortening.

claim: Neurites from π-EB1 i3Neurons were repelled by blue light barriers placed in front of the growth cone while control i3Neurons were unaffected.

claim: A novel approach is presented to replace the central MT regulator EB1 with a photosensitive variant by inserting a light-sensitive protein interaction module encoded by a short genetic cassette into an inter-domain linker by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing.
source: In summary, we present a novel approach to replace the central MT regulator EB1 with a photosensitive variant by inserting a light-sensitive protein interaction module encoded by a short genetic cassette – that we named π-element – into an inter-domain linker by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing.
evidence: This is a summary of the methodological contribution of the manuscript.

claim: The π-element only needs to contain ORFs encoding LOV2 and Zdk1 and the required regulatory elements, while the flanking homology arms direct it to the correct genomic locus.
source: It is important to note that the π-element only needs to contain ORFs encoding LOV2 and Zdk1 and the required regulatory elements, while the flanking homology arms direct it to the correct genomic locus.
evidence: This is a description of the π-element design.

claim: The rest of the protein of interest remains encoded by the endogenous gene when using the π-element approach.
source: The rest of the protein of interest remains encoded by the endogenous gene.
evidence: This is a description of the π-element approach.

claim: A similar strategy to the π-element approach could be adapted to many other multidomain proteins.
source: Here, we also include a fluorescent protein tag to monitor π-EB1 photodissociation and a leucine zipper coiled-coil to retain dimerization of the π-EB1 N-terminal half during blue light exposure. While we demonstrate the utility of this approach for the MAPRE1 gene in hiPSCs, we believe that a similar strategy could be adapted to many other multidomain proteins supplementing the optogenetic toolbox to investigate localized protein functions in real-time (Wittmann et al., 2020), but it should be noted that photodissociation kinetics may be different with monomeric proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of the method with a reference.

claim: Photodissociation kinetics may be different with monomeric proteins when using the π-element approach.
source: Here, we also include a fluorescent protein tag to monitor π-EB1 photodissociation and a leucine zipper coiled-coil to retain dimerization of the π-EB1 N-terminal half during blue light exposure. While we demonstrate the utility of this approach for the MAPRE1 gene in hiPSCs, we believe that a similar strategy could be adapted to many other multidomain proteins supplementing the optogenetic toolbox to investigate localized protein functions in real-time (Wittmann et al., 2020), but it should be noted that photodissociation kinetics may be different with monomeric proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat for applying the method to monomeric proteins.

source: The LOV2/Zdk1 module interacts in the dark, which is opposite to all other optogenetic dimerization modules and therefore, enables an unperturbed dark state and acute functional knockout of a given protein activity through blue light exposure.
evidence: This is stated as a key feature of the LOV2/Zdk1 module.

claim: Replacing an endogenous protein with a photosensitive variant in a single genome editing step has important advantages by allowing modification of proteins for which genetic knockouts might be lethal.
source: Thus, replacing an endogenous protein with a photosensitive variant in a single genome editing step as presented here has important advantages by allowing modification of proteins for which genetic knockouts might be lethal and further enabling optogenetics in complex cell systems that are not amenable to transient genetic manipulations.

claim: Unchanged F-actin polymerization dynamics during blue light indicate that retraction likely results from a loss of growth cone adhesion or an increase in neurite actomyosin contractility consistent with MT-shortening induced RhoA activation.
source: Although we do not completely dissect the molecular mechanism underlying the π-EB1 photodissociation-mediated neurite retraction response, unchanged F-actin polymerization dynamics during blue light indicate that retraction likely results from a loss of growth cone adhesion or an increase in neurite actomyosin contractility consistent with MT-shortening induced RhoA activation (Joo and Olson, 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results with reference to previous literature.

claim: An increase in neurite contractility that does not remain localized to the region of blue light exposure may explain the difficulty in using π-EB1 photodissociation to control growth cone guidance more precisely.

claim: Optogenetic tools that provide attractive stimuli could be a promising avenue to control growth cone guidance.
source: Thus, although other optogenetic tools that provide attractive stimuli could be a promising avenue to control growth cone guidance (Harris et al., 2020), inhibitory stimuli that induce MT depolymerization may be too difficult to control to be practically useful in synthetic biology approaches building defined neuron networks.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion with reference to previous literature.
